processing: Made as Ceylon black tea: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried. Little is documented about methods specific to this district, so this is the general pattern of the class.
harvest_season: Ceylon tea gardens pick through much of the year; which picking is best in this district is poorly documented in plain terms, so ask the seller for the date.
appearance_dry: As with other Ceylon black teas, dark brown to near-black leaf, usually sorted into broken or whole-leaf grades.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear reddish amber, as with other hill-grown Ceylon blacks.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown pieces of leaf, as is usual for orthodox Ceylon black tea.
taste_profile: Expect what is typical of Ceylon hill blacks: brisk, clean and fairly bright, with light malt. Notes specific to this district are not well recorded.

brewing.notes: Western-style, as is usual for Ceylon black tea. Shorten the steep if it turns astringent; a splash of milk works with the stronger broken grades.

vintage_note: Usual for Ceylon black tea: sold by district and leaf grade rather than by vintage, and best drunk within a year or two of production. It does not improve with age, so a recent packing date matters more than any year on the label.
description:
Uda Pussellawa is a tea district in the Sri Lankan hills, sold under its own name as a Ceylon black tea. Little is written about it in the sources read here.

The tea is made the way Ceylon black tea generally is: the leaf is withered, rolled, oxidised all the way and dried. That is what gives the class its reddish cup and its grip.

In the cup, expect what is typical of hill-grown Ceylon rather than a well-mapped house style: a brisk, clean black tea with some malt. Brew it Western-style in water just off the boil, and pull it early if you drink it without milk.

When buying, look for the district named on the pack, along with the garden and grade if the seller gives them. A plain 'Ceylon' label tells you nothing about where the leaf grew.
history: Little is documented in detail about how tea developed in this district. One trace of the area's colonial past is the Uda Pussellawa Railway, a narrow-gauge line that ran from Nanu Oya through Nuwara Eliya to Ragala between 1903 and 1948.
